> The upoddhāta (the preliminary) faces the opponents who deny the self's lordship. The Cārvāka
> (materialist) cannot even frame a refutation, having no means of proof; the Sāṃkhya (the many selfs,
> or one self with hidden lordship) is not wholly far. The real pūrvapakṣin is the Buddhist
> (Sautrāntika/Vijñānavādin), who denies the self outright. Against him Abhinavagupta must establish
> that the self is the Lord.
>
> The Cārvāka, lacking a stance of their own, cannot refute the other side without entering the means-
> of-proof conventions, in which they lose their Cārvāka-ness. So the Sautrāntika is the pūrvapakṣin
> here; those who accept the self — the many or the one with hidden lordship — are nearer.

> (kriyā) is impossible too. Kārikā 9: the action of a body is the coming-to-be of this and that
> place-and-the-rest; it is not other, from the unseen (adṛṣṭa); nor is it one — for the ordered (the
> sequence) of the one is not fit. One action cannot be at once this place and that; a single action

> The Buddhist's pūrvapakṣa has denied the self, the cognition, and the action. Now it completes itself:

> How, if the manifestation has no touch of time, do we remember yesterday? The pastness is not a real
> quality of the object; it is the *being-previously-manifested*. The one light, contracting under the
> upādhis of place and time ("yesterday, thirsty, with that friend"), appears as the past. Memory is the
> re-apprehension of what was previously manifested.
>
> The yogin, by the discipline, thins the body and the other's cognition shines in its own place. And
> the deepest point: cognition is self-cognition (svasaṃvitti) — self-luminous, distinguishing it from
> the inert — and because it is self-cognition, it is free to manifest the other.

> The yogin knows another's cognition. But a cognition can never be the *object* of another cognition —
> for the two would have to stand in the relation of object and holder. Abhinavagupta analyzes what
> "being an object" means: a thing is an object when the awareness assimilates its form (the sārūpya),
> which requires the object to be both like and unlike the cognition. But a cognition has no such
> difference from another: their form is the self-luminous awareness, which has nothing in it to be set
> over against another awareness. Two mirrors can reflect one another; two cognitions cannot.
>
> The cognition is self-luminous, never made the object of another — the knower is the ajaḍa, the
> not-inert. This establishes the conscious knower, with which the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi closes.

> The jñānaśakti (the knowledge-power) is the capacity by which anything is known. Its central claim:
> the manifestation is the very form of the objects. Their being *is* their being-manifested; to know a

>
> The essence of the manifestation is the reflexive-awareness: the light that knows itself in knowing
> the object.

> The external object has been shown to be un-establishable — neither as a whole nor as atoms. The
> objector asks how this is so, since the external was earlier inferred from the variety of the
> appearance-order. Abhinavagupta answers with the īśvarādvaya: the external is not needed, because the
> Lord manifests the whole world from within himself, by his own will, without an external material
> cause — as a yogin does. The decisive image is the dream. The Buddhist had used the dream to prove the
> world's unreality (it appears without a cause). Abhinavagupta accepts that the dream is uncaused, but
> draws the opposite conclusion: the dream shows that consciousness alone can create an object-mass by
> its will.
>
> The passage establishes the īśvarādvaya — the Lord manifests from within.

> The valid means (pramāṇa) is not a separate instrument over against the knower; it is the knower's own
> operation (pramātṛ-vyāpāra). The five objects of perception and non-perception, thrown into the one
> consciousness-ocean, are joined by the freedom-wave; the one appearance is the cause-and-effect
> appearance; and the re-recollection is the knower's operation. As the Mukuta-saṃhitā says, the joiner
> alone is the means.
>
> In memory (kārikā 5), that very self-consciousness is the valid means — "that alone, not another."
> Memory does not bring a new thing; it re-grasps what was already grasped. The memory is the prior
> experience, self-conscious, remembered.

> The passage closes the jñānādhikāra with the unity of the knowers. Kārikā 10: the whole dealing of
> the world — the path by which consciousnesses know, remember, and act together — would be impossible
> if the consciousnesses were mutually opaque streams; but the dealing is, so the consciousnesses must
> be one. The unity is argued via the dealing, not by a bare assertion of identity. The Sāṃkhya's
> separate puruṣa is then re-read: it is not another self but the un-recognized own-lordship, the
> contracted consciousness.
>
> Kārikā 11 draws the conclusion: the great-Lordship is nothing but the reflexive awareness. The
> Lordship is not a fifth power added to the four; it is what the four are. The powers reduce to the
> self-awareness, and the self-awareness is the Lord.

> The kriyādhikāra opens a paradox: the Lord is beyond time and sequence, yet the world is shot through
> with sequence. How can the timeless act in time? The homage answers: Śiva, "though free of sequence,
> manifests manifold sequences." The image is the mirror: a mirror bears countless reflections without
> ceasing to be the one, undivided mirror. So the one consciousness can take up seemingly contradictory
> forms without its oneness being divided. This is the action-support (kriyāśraya): the one that acts is
> one, and because it is one it can show sequence at all.

> The cognitions of action, relation, universal, substance, direction and time have a substrate that is
> at once one and many, and they are accepted as true — true by their stability and true by their
> efficacy. The example: the body of Caitra — and of Maitra — although it differs by place, time, and
> shape, shines forth without abandoning its oneness, in the recognition "this is the very same body."
> That unity is the action, in the judgment "Caitra is walking." The substrate is both one (the unity of
> the recognition) and many (the differences) — the bhedābheda.

and efficacy.

> The passage asks what really makes a cognition valid. Ordinary discourse appears to locate the
> validating force in the object itself: a cognition of blue is stable because the blue object
> determines it. Abhinavagupta argues that this cannot be sufficient. If the object possessed this
> determining force simply in itself, its appearance would not be restricted to one subject rather than
> another. Its manifestation therefore depends upon consciousness. He then pushes the argument further:
> knower, means of knowledge, and known object are not ultimately three independently functioning
> factors, but aspects of a single manifestation or "light." The point of the passage is thus to
> relocate the operation of *pramāṇa* from an independently existing object to the event of
> manifestatio

> If the valid means seizes only an appearance, how can it reach the single thing those appearances
> belong to? The answer is the *synthesizing awareness* (anusandhāna) — the one reflective grasp that
> gathers the many appearances into one. The jar is divided by viewpoint, wish, and convention — long,
> round, upright, a being, a substance, a jar — yet the synthesis keeps it one. And the object-action
> makes a thing real: separate lamp-lights, gathered in one house, do one thing (they make it bright);
> streams, falling into the ocean, do one thing. The doer of one object-action must be one.

> If the means seizes only appearances, how do we tell true from false — the real jar from the illusory
> double-moon or the shell-mistaken-for-silver? Abhinavagupta's answer: error is a matter of the
> reflexive-awareness; the distinction is made not by the pramāṇa's being un-contradicted but by the
> *reflexive-awareness'* being un-contradicted. The thing I saw far off as a whole, I now see near with
> its details; it is one by the one recognition "this is the very thing I saw before." The shell-silver
> has no standing as the real silver. In the end it is the knower who is the ground of everything.

shell-silver.

> The vimarśa closes on how one attains the Lord: by the Lord's grace, through a fourfold effort — the
> initiatory rite (dīkṣā), the vision-yoga (dhyāna), knowledge (jñāna), and devotion (bhāvanā). The
> order matters: knowledge is preceded by initiation; and if one has not practiced the vision-yoga,
> there is devotion. And the prāṇa's being felt as "I" is not a conflict with the param-ātman — the two
> are present together; the param-ātman shines freely, and by that shining the prāṇa appears as "I."

> The relation between the known and the knower has been shown to be the expansion of the action-power.
> Now Abhinavagupta turns to cause and effect: the essence of cause and effect is nothing but the
> relation of agent and object of action. Causality is the agency of a conscious knower. The Lord
> manifests the world by his will — the un-divided, un-ordered will tinted by the particular thing to be
> made. And the inert cannot cause: the seed cannot endow the sprout with being (it is either existent,
> and nothing is acquired, or non-existent, and cannot come to be). The potter creates the pot by his
> power; the yogin by his will alone.

> The Vijñānavādin objects: if everything is appearance, cause and effect are only relations between
> appearances, and an un-manifested fire is nothing — so how can the smoke arise from it and be
> inferred? Abhinavagupta answers with the one creation: the Lord creates the appearances *for all the
> knowers at once, as one*. So the pervasion (smoke implies fire) belongs to every knower alike; the
> fire-appearance, indirect to the one who infers, is the "cause of the Lord" (adhipatipratyaya).
> Inference holds across knowers because the appearances are created as one. And the dependence of cause
> and effect is not a real otherness: the fire and its heat are one, joined by the synthesis.

> The sharpest objection to the unity: if consciousness is one and the difference of things is mere
> ignorance, how is action possible? For action needs an agent and an object, distinct; but if all is

> The kriyādhikāra showed that the action-power's form is the un-clouded manifestation of all the
> categories. But what are these categories, the tattvas? Perception is not an omniscient eye; inference
> lacks the pervasion that would reach everything. Only the āgama — the revealed teaching — can measure
> the whole. And at the heart of it is the Śivatattva, the body of every category: cause-effect rests
> not in the inert but in the consciousness-form, whose essence is manifestation-and-reflexive-awareness.
> Knowledge and action — manifestation and reflexivity — are inseparable; this pair is the supreme form
> of all beings.

> Descending to the bound knower, the pure self is covered by the kañcukas (the "armours"): niyati
> (fixity), kāla (time), rāga (attachment), vidyā (limited knowledge), kalā (limited agency). Take
> niyati: the seed is the cause of the sprout, not of the pot — the apparent fixing of each effect to
> its own cause. But this fixity belongs to the knower, not the known; in reality the Lord alone shines
> forth as "this is the cause of that," and the binding is a covering laid over the reality by the
> limited knower. The bound knower is the māyīya knower, facing the distinct things of the world, which
> are counted as twenty-three categories of the known.

> The dvitīyo vimarśa examines the knowers, for the recognition of the Lord in the self is the heart of
> the śāstra. The homage is to the one "who wields the trident, cutting the three nooses" — the three
> stains (mala): āṇava (finitude), māyīya (objectivity), kārma (action). The bound knower, the paśu, is
> blind by māyā, wandering in saṃsāra, bound by his actions; he has lost the freedom of the awareness.
> Over against him stands the pati, the Lord, whose own-members are his own.

> The bound knower lives in a round of states. At the lowest extreme is the void: the pralayākala, the
> dissolved knower, with only the barest trace of an "I" — a sleep without a dream. With the breath
> come the three great states: deep sleep (suṣupta, with the vidyākalā / pralayākala grades), the dream
> (svapna, the mind's own making, refuted by the waking), and waking (jāgrat, the common creation shared
> by all the knowers). The states are the descent of the Lord through the forms of the world.

> The tattvasaṅgraha (the collection of the essence) opens with the single great claim: the own-self
> alone of all beings is the one Lord, the maheśvara. His re-recollection — "I, this" — is un-broken.
> But then how does the many arise? In the own-self, by the Lord's freedom, a "this-part" is created,
> preceded by a contraction; and by the this-ness of the distinct-known, an "I-being" shines, the
> grasper. He who says "I am happy," grasping himself as this contracted being — that is the bound one.
> And his liberation is precisely the recognition of what he truly is.

grasper.

> The bound one's creation is *un-common* (asādhāraṇī) — private, per-knower, per-moment, vanishing with
> him — yet sustained by the Lord's creation (īśasṛṣṭyujīvinī). The whole difference of bound and
> liberated hangs on one fact: the bound one does not *know* his own power; he forgets that the world he
> builds is built with the Lord's own materials. The construction-action is the bond — by it the
> māyā-power binds the animal; even the "free" constructions ("I, the king, stand") are other-dependent.
> And there is a path out: the abandonment of construction. When the bound one comes to the "I-this" of
